newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha looks to new term as Albania foments.
newsitem.headline: Berisha looks to new term as Albania foments.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha, facing weeks of protests over dubious investment schemes, was certain to be re-selected by his right-wing Democratic Party this week to stand for a fresh five-year term as head of state.

Berisha, a 52-year-old former heart surgeon, has to seek re-election by parliament by mid-March but there is little doubt he will be returned to power by an assembly dominated by Democrats after last year's disputed general election.

Despite the certainty, Berisha toured the Balkan state of 3.4 million people last week in an attempt to drum up support following anti-government demonstrations, many of them violent, sparked by the crash of pyramid investment schemes in January.

On Sunday, around 5,000 marchers staged a noisy but peaceful protest in the southern port of Vlore for a 19th day to demand the dismissal of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government over its handling of the investment scandal.
The demonstrators rallied in front of Vlore university to express support for 53 students inside who have been on hunger strike since Thursday.

Thousands of impoverished Albanians lost their savings, many of them after selling homes and businesses to pour cash into the schemes offering up to 60 percent interest a month. Officials estimate $1 to $2 billion could have been lost in the schemes.

Five of the investment scams have collapsed leaving many savers destitute. Thousands of ordinary people have turned their anger on Berisha and Meksi, blaming them for failing to regulate the schemes or warning investors about the potential dangers of losing their cash.
The government has repeatedly said there will be no reimbursement from the state, already burdened by a huge deficit.

Berisha has told hapless investors they had learned a hard lesson from the country's recent embrace of capitalism. The pyramids used cash from new investors to pay interest as high as 60 percent a month to earlier investors before collapsing.
There was more bad news on Sunday for investors in one of the collapsed schemes, Gjallica, from a state commission set up to investigate the scandal.
Commission head Blerim Cela told state television that it had identified around $28 million of Gjallica's assets to cover the outstanding $145 million owed to thousands of investors.
The relatively prosperous south has been particularly hard hit by the collapse of the pyramid schemes and the region around Vlore invested heavily in the Gjallica fund.
The couple who ran the fund have fled Albania but they have been charged with fraud along with 20 other defendants.
"How can the government which was in power during the theft be trusted to make sure the money is returned?" asked protester Engjell Dine. "We're determined to keep going."
"All of our families invested in Gjallica and they lost all their savings. It has affected the lives of everyone in Vlore," student leader Leonard Kajtalli told Reuters.

Addressing a crowd of supporters in the northern city of Shkoder on Saturday, Berisha blamed the main opposition Socialist Party for exploiting the unrest -- the worst crisis to face Berisha and the Democrats since they won power in 1992.

The Socialists changed their name from the Communist Party after Albania emerged from 45 years of ruthless Stalinist isolation in 1990 when there were no banks, no interest rates and no pyramid schemes.
